content: The joule, denoted by the symbol J, is the SI unit of energy. It is named after James Prescott Joule, who conducted pioneering work on the interrelationship between heat, electricity, and mechanical work. One joule is defined as the amount of work done or energy expended when a force of one newton moves an object one meter in the direction of the force. This is also expressed as a newton-meter, symbolized as N·m. However, it is important to note that while torque shares the same unit (N·m) as work, the two quantities are fundamentally different. In terms of elementary units, one joule can also be described as: The work required to move an electric charge of one coulomb through an electrical potential difference of one volt, which is expressed as one coulomb-volt (C·V). The work done to produce a power output of one watt continuously for one second, also referred to as one watt-second (W·s). This is comparable to the kilowatt-hour, a larger unit of energy. The value of the joule was determined through experiments conducted by James Prescott Joule, which demonstrated the mechanical equivalent of heat. The term joule was first introduced by Dr. Mayer of Heilbronn. In terms of conversions, one joule is exactly equal to 10^7 ergs. It is also useful to remember that: 1 joule = 1 newton-meter = 1 watt-second. In everyday contexts, one joule is approximately: The energy required to lift a small apple one meter vertically. The energy released when that same apple falls one meter to the ground. The amount of heat energy a quiet person generates every hundredth of a second. The energy required to heat one gram of dry, cool air by 1 degree Celsius. One hundredth of the energy a person can obtain by consuming a single drop of beer.
